..
Issued at 344 PM CST Wed Nov 25 2026

...Synopsis...

Water vapor imagery reveals shortwave ridging aloft over the
Northern Plains and Upper Midwest with broader southwest and 
more moist flow out of the Pacific Northwest and Northern
Rockies. This will help bring a warmer air mass into our region
starting Thanksgiving Day. At the surface, a somewhat tightened
pressure gradient will help south winds stay elevated tonight -
mitigating the potential for fog.

Thanksgiving Day will be mild and dry with the help of surface
ridging and southwesterly/zonal flow aloft advecting warmer air
mass into the region from the west. Temperatures are forecast in
the 40s, along with a mix of clouds and sunshine. Impactful
weather is not anticipated Thanksgiving Day.

Toward Friday into Saturday, a well advertised upper low is 
forecast to emanate from the southwesterly/zonal flow out of 
the Pacific Northwest into the southern Canadian Prairie 
Provinces. While the majority of forcing from this upper low 
will stay in Canada, it does bring attendant frontal boundaries
and eventually a relatively cooler air mass (Saturday) into our
region. The first frontal boundary will be on the leading edge 
of increasing moisture Friday morning. This brings a chance for 
light rain and/or wintry mix. Should precipitation come in the 
form of wintry mix, there is potential for travel impacts Friday
morning.

Temperatures markedly warm Friday afternoon, with well above
average temperatures well into the 40s. Some locations in
eastern ND and the Red River Valley are likely to touch 50 
degrees, too.

A cold front sweeps through late Friday into Saturday, with a
relatively cooler air mass bringing temperatures back toward
average - although still above average high temperatures near or
above freezing. Within the post-frontal air mass, cold air
advection and lingering vorticity aloft associated with the
nearby upper low allows for a chance to see rain and/or snow
showers. Precip rates during this time are currently expected 
to be light enough to mitigate potential for wintry impacts
Saturday.

Getting into next week, overall zonal flow aloft with embedded
upper ridging/troughing wave packets traversing east through the
flow is expected. This may allow for bouts of transient
precipitation, including rain and snow. At this time, however,
confidence is low in evolution of synoptic features next week,
translating to low confidence in chance for impactful weather
next week. That being said, there are no glaring signals for 
significantly impactful weather. Additionally, there are no
signals for significant swings in air masses, with majority of
our air mass emanating from the west. This would indicate that
relatively above average temperatures will continue into next
week.

...Low chance for travel impacts Friday morning...

Most modeled guidance indicates potential for a north-south 
oriented band of precipitation to traverse west to east across 
the region. Low level temperatures are close enough to freezing 
where precipitation could fall in the form of wintry mix of 
freezing rain and/or snow/snow pellets. The majority of guidance
also indicates in at least some low level dryness to help 
evaporate/sublimate some precipitation before it reaches the 
ground - but perhaps not all of the precipitation. This means 
the degree of forcing for precipitation production will be 
important as there will need to be sufficient amount of forcing 
to generate rates high enough to survive the dry layer. However,
confidence in the degree of forcing aloft is low based on 
differences offered by modeled guidance. Additionally, 
uncertainty continues to stem from low level temperatures. 
Temperatures may be just below or just above freezing during the
passage of this precipitation. Should temperatures be just 
above freezing, rain will be favored. Conversely, wintry mix 
will be favored if temperatures are near or just below freezing.
Thus, confidence in wintry mix leading to impacts remains low.

While there are uncertainties mentioned above, there is fairly 
high confidence in the window of impact potential shutting down 
by late morning as temperatures surge well above freezing by the
afternoon. Also, accumulation/accretion will be light given the
brevity of precipitation over any one particular location given
how "thin" the band will be as well as its steady pace 
eastward. So the scenario that would lead to travel impacts 
comes in the form of light icing from wintry mix Friday morning 
due to temperatures near or just below freezing as well as 
enough precipitation being generated aloft to survive the low 
level dry layer. Seems pretty conditional right? Despite this, 
it is within the realm of possibility, and may come as a 
surprise due to its seemingly innocuous look on modeled 
guidance. Remember, it only takes a glaze of ice to create 
travel impacts.
